title: Am I my brother's keeper (Genesis 4:1–16)
hook: Cain kills Abel and God still puts a mark of protection on him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the protoevangelium: a promise tucked inside the serpent's sentence. Your line was the promise came first. Now, outside the garden, the first family.

A line from Genesis gets quoted far from Genesis. A politician uses it in a speech. A teacher writes it on a board. Someone mutters it when asked to help a neighbor: what am I, my brother's keeper? It sounds like a shrug. In Genesis, it's a lie, told to God's face, by a man who has just killed his brother. Two brothers, born outside Eden. One works the soil, one keeps sheep. They both bring an offering. And one of them doesn't come home.
screen: `A LINE PEOPLE QUOTE.` → `IT'S A LIE, TOLD TO GOD.` → `TWO BROTHERS, ONE OFFERING EACH.`

segments.voice: First, the offerings. Cain brings fruit of the ground; Abel brings the firstlings of his flock. God has respect to Abel's offering and not to Cain's. Why? Genesis is silent, and readers have offered guesses; the Letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith. Second, the warning. Cain's face falls, and God speaks to him before anything happens: sin lies at the door, but you can master it. Cain doesn't answer. He takes his brother into the field and kills him. Third, the question. As in the garden, God asks what God already knows. In the Douay-Rheims: "Where is thy brother Abel? And he answered, I know not: am I my brother's keeper?" Adam hid. Cain lies, then shrugs. And God says: "The voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." The ground that took Adam's sweat now drinks a brother's blood. The Catechism quotes this scene when it teaches the sacredness of every human life. Fourth, the surprise. Cain is sent out as a wanderer, afraid someone will kill him, and God puts a mark on him: not a brand of shame, but a sign of protection. Nobody is to take his life. Even for a murderer, God keeps the door open. Catholics remember Abel at the altar: the Roman Canon names the offering of Abel the just. Genesis leaves Cain's question hanging. Readers hear the rest of scripture answer it: yes.
screen: `WHY ABEL'S? THE TEXT IS SILENT.` · `SIN LIES AT THE DOOR.` · `THY BROTHER'S BLOOD CRIETH.` · `A MARK OF PROTECTION.` · then, large: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: Let the face of a brother or sister come to mind, by blood or someone who's been one to you, and ask where they are this week and what's hard for them right now. If there's distance between you, notice it without blaming anyone, and just hold them. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Shomer, Hebrew for keeper, one who watches over: Cain's lie and shrug when God asked where his brother was. Today's word.
Your line: yes, you are. Cain's shrug doesn't get the last word. That's day three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, the priest asks God to accept the offering as he accepted the gifts of Abel the just, the sacrifice of Abraham and the offering of Melchizedek.

chat.says: Isn't "am I my brother's keeper" just a fair way of saying not my business?
options: In Genesis it's Cain's lie to cover a murder, and scripture answers: yes, you are.
In Genesis it's Abel's question, asking God why his brother hated him so.
It's God's question to Cain, telling him to keep an eye on his little brother.
